It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population.
Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret.
For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use.
This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends.
Newer studies are being published on these topics, including a recent ABCD study in which problematic social media use and depressive symptoms predicted each other over time.
Our study aims to contribute more broadly, by looking at gaming as well as social media, at hours and problematic use in the same participants, and at brain measures alongside symptoms.
ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) offered a chance for us to look at these together, since it profiles neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical measures in the same participants.

In this preregistered multimodal study, our goal was to see how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity.
All five confirmatory associations were positive but marginal (β = 0.051 to 0.173), and changed little across several robustness checks.
In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were.
The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants.
More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ.
In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly.
Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself.
Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study.
We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

Screen use for adolescents has only increased over the years, from schoolwork to games and keeping in touch with friends, and questions about how this use relates to well-being and brain development have only grown.
Large cohort studies have mostly found small associations.
In the ABCD Study, a typical association between screen time and mental health is around r = 0.05, and an above-average one is around r = 0.09 (Nagata et al., 2024).

Beyond the preregistered tests, we ran three exploratory analyses.
First, to see which measure tends to change first within participants, we used cross-lagged models.
We tested whether SMAQ or VGAQ at one visit predicted attention or DSM ADHD problems at a later visit, and whether these problems predicted later SMAQ or VGAQ.
This was done from year 2 to year 3, year 2 to year 4, and year 3 to year 4.

The tests were then corrected within each lag.
Second, we looked at the emotion and reward tasks, to see if they related to ADHD symptoms or to problematic use.
For this, we used the emotional n-back and reward task measures provided in the release.
We only analyzed sessions that passed the release's quality and inclusion flags.
Brain measures were also adjusted for head motion during tasks.
We also looked at emotional n-back, which measures accuracy and reaction time in remembering faces if their expression appeared emotional (positive and negative) vs neutral.
We also used amygdala and insula activation to emotional faces.
Fusiform activation to faces compared with places was included as a check, since faces should clearly activate this region.
From the reward task, we used how much more quickly participants responded when they could win or lose money, compared with trials where nothing was at stake.
We also used accumbens activation while participants waited for a possible reward and when they saw the result, and medial orbitofrontal activation when they saw the result.

Several limitations are worth keeping in mind when considering these results.
Since the data are observational, these associations cannot be interpreted as causal.
While cross-lagged models can test whether single measures predict later change in other measures, they cannot rule out other factors that affect both (Heffer et al., 2019).

text.text: All outcomes were parent-rated too.
Parents may see things differently than the adolescents themselves, and may miss experiences that participants cannot yet put into words, or that have not shown up yet developmentally.
Teacher reports only covered a smaller sample, and youth self-reports were not collected at baseline, so we left these out of this analysis.
SMAQ and VGAQ could only survey year 2 participants with social media accounts or who played video games respectively.
Screen time was also self-reported in hours, without the preregistered 18-hour cap.
Self-reported hours may also differ from what phones record.
Likewise, many participants scored at the lowest value of each symptom scale, from 39.4% to 69.3% and 54.5% on the ADHD scale, which limits how much these scores can vary.
We used total SMAQ and VGAQ scores instead of single items, since looking at each item or at patterns of answers would add many comparisons.
Our goal was to first see if the preregistered total scores relate to symptoms, yet item-level patterns and profiles of problematic use can still be explored in future work.
When non-users were given the lowest score, the link between SMAQ and attention problems dropped from 0.107 to 0.042.
Every association remained positive, in the same direction.
So the H1 finding may mostly apply to adolescents who already use social media.
Our estimates were also unweighted.
They describe the ABCD sample, and may not carry over to a broader population.
We were also limited by the brain data resolution.
The structural associations were very small and cross-sectional, and we did not have the computing resources to analyze the detailed parcel-level connectome data.
This study focuses on 338 network-level edges, though future work could extend this to greater resolution.
Since there were only 100 permutations, our smallest p-values were also limited to 0.010.
Our analysis also differs from the preregistration in a few places, such as using release 7.0 (Table 4).
